title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 70 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 446–448 (Night 70, continuing directly from nights-69; the print itself numbers this night “69” again), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 70 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Sharkān, having read the king's letter, sends his sister's daughter (the learned slave-girl) to Baghdad under the chamberlain's escort, with the tribute of Damascus and a letter, while his own daughter, Quḍiya-fa-kān, wears the bead on a gold chain. Ḍawʾ al-Makān, the stoker's companion, sees the caravan pass and, hearing whose it is, weeps for home and sets out with it, the stoker following him. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and the sixty,
sentences.i: And when it was the seventieth night,
sentences.n: The print numbers this night التاسعة والستون, “the sixty-ninth”, which is the number of the night before; it is a compositor’s repeat and the count here is the seventieth. The label is kept as printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَ عُمَرَ بْنَ النُّعْمَانِ قَالَ فِي مَكْتُوبِهِ وَأَرْسَلَ إِلَيْنَا الْجَارِيَةَ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تُنَاظِرَ هُنَّ بَيْنَ الْعُلَمَاءِ فَإِذَا غَلَبَتْهُنَّ أَرْسَلْتَهَا إِلَيْكَ وَصَحِبْتَهَا خَرَاجَ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika ʿUmara ibna al-Nuʿmāni qāla fī maktūbihi wa-arsala ilaynā al-jāriyata li-ajli an tunāẓira hunna bayna al-ʿulamāʾi fa-idhā ghalabathunna arsaltahā ilayka wa-ṣaḥibtahā kharāja Baghdāda
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that the king ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān said in his letter — and he sent to us the slave-girl — for the sake that she contend-with them among the learned: and if she overcomes them, you send her to you, and you accompany her with the tribute of Baghdad.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān said in his letter — and he sent the slave-girl to us — that she was to be set to debate the old woman and her scholars among the learned men, and that if she defeated them, we should send her on to him, and send the tribute of Baghdad with her.
sentences.n: The print runs السعيد and أن together (al-saʿīdu anna); kept as printed. The grammar of the letter is loose: the king’s words are given indirectly, and the pronouns of the sentence (“you send her to you”) slide between the king’s voice and the reporter’s; the idiomatic layer straightens them. تناظر هن is printed as two words; it is read as tunāẓira hunna, “that she debate them” (the five scholars), and the verb ارسلتها, vocalised as a second-person form following the letter’s address, is rendered as “we should send her”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَلِمَ بِذَلِكَ شَرْكَانُ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى صِهْرِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ هَاتِ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي زَوَّجْتُكَ إِيَّاهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿalima bi-dhālika Sharkānu aqbala ʿalā ṣihrihi wa-qāla lahu hāti al-jāriyata allatī zawwajtuka iyyāhā
sentences.l: And when Sharkān knew of that, he turned toward his son-in-law and said to him: Bring the slave-girl whom I married you to her.
sentences.i: When Sharkān learned of this, he turned to his son-in-law and said, “Bring me the girl I married to you.”

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا حَضَرَتْ أَوْقَفَهَا عَلَى الْكِتَابِ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا أُخْتِي مَا عِنْدَكِ مِنَ الرَّأْيِ فِي رَدِّ الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ḥaḍarat awqafahā ʿalā al-kitābi wa-qāla lahā yā ukhtī mā ʿindaki mina al-raʾyi fī raddi al-jawābi
sentences.l: And when she was present, he made her stand upon the letter, and said to her: O my sister, what is with you of opinion in the returning of the answer?
sentences.i: When she came, he let her read the letter and said to her, “My sister, what do you think we should answer?”
sentences.n: أوقفها على الكتاب is literally “made her stand upon the letter”, that is, made her acquainted with it.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ لَهُ الرَّأْيُ رَأْيُكَ ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لَهُ وَقَدِ اشْتَاقَتْ إِلَى أَهْلِهَا وَوَطَنِهَا أَرْسِلْنِي صُحْبَةَ زَوْجِي الْحَاجِبِ لِأَحْكِيَ لِأَبِي حِكَايَتِي وَأُخْبِرَهُ بِمَاوَقَعَ لِي مَعَ الْبَدَوِيِّ الَّذِي بَاعَنِي لِلتَّاجِرِ وَأُخْبِرَهُ بِأَنَّ التَّاجِرَ بَاعَنِي لَكَ وَأَنْتَ زَوَّجْتَنِي لِلْحَاجِبِ بَعْدَ عِتْقِي
sentences.tr: qālat lahu al-raʾyu raʾyuka thumma qālat lahu wa-qadi ishtāqat ilā ahlihā wa-waṭanihā arsilnī ṣuḥbata zawjī al-ḥājibi li-aḥkiya li-abī ḥikāyatī wa-ukhbirahu bi-mā waqaʿa lī maʿa al-badawiyyi alladhī bāʿanī li-al-tājiri wa-ukhbirahu bi-anna al-tājira bāʿanī laka wa-anta zawwajtanī li-al-ḥājibi baʿda ʿitqī
sentences.l: She said to him: The opinion is your opinion. Then she said to him — and she had longed for her family and her homeland — Send me in the company of my husband the chamberlain, that I may tell my father my story, and inform him of what befell me with the Bedouin who sold me to the merchant, and inform him that the merchant sold me to you, and you married me to the chamberlain after my freeing.
sentences.i: She said, “The decision is yours.” Then, longing for her family and her homeland, she said, “Send me with my husband the chamberlain, so that I may tell my father my story and tell him what happened to me with the Bedouin who sold me to the merchant — and that the merchant sold me to you, and that you married me to the chamberlain after I was freed.”
sentences.n: The print runs بما and وقع together (bimāwaqaʿa); kept as printed.

sentences.l: And Sharkān said to her: And it is so.
sentences.i: Sharkān said to her, “So be it.”

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ شَرْكَانُ ابْنَتَهُ قُضِىَ فَكَانَ وَسَلَّمَهَا لِلْمَرَاضِعِ وَالْخَدَمِ وَشَرَعَ فِي تَجْهِيزِ الْخَرَاجِ وَأَعْطَاهُ لِلْحَاجِبِ وَأَمَرَهُ بِالسَّيْرِ مَعَ الْجَارِيَةِ وَالْخَرَاجِ إِلَى بَغْدَادَوَرَسَمَ لَهُ بِمَحَفَّةٍ يَجْلِسُ فِيهَا وَالْجَارِيَةِ بِمَحَفَّةٍ أُخْرَى
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha Sharkānu ibnatahu Quḍiya-fa-kāna wa-sallamahā li-al-marāḍiʿi wa-al-khadami wa-sharaʿa fī tajhīzi al-kharāji wa-aʿṭāhu li-al-ḥājibi wa-amarahu bi-al-sayri maʿa al-jāriyati wa-al-kharāji ilā Baghdāda wa-rasama lahu bi-maḥaffatin yajlisu fīhā wa-al-jāriyati bi-maḥaffatin ukhrā
sentences.l: And Sharkān took his daughter It-was-decreed-and-it-was, and handed her to the wet-nurses and the servants, and set about the equipping of the tribute, and gave it to the chamberlain, and commanded him with the going with the slave-girl and the tribute to Baghdad; and he appointed for him a litter in which he would sit, and the slave-girl a litter other.
sentences.i: Sharkān took his daughter Quḍiya-fa-kān and handed her to the wet-nurses and the servants. He set about preparing the tribute, gave it into the chamberlain’s charge, and ordered him to travel with the girl and the tribute to Baghdad, assigning him one litter to ride in and the girl another.
sentences.n: قضي فكان, “It was decreed, and it came to be”, is the name Sharkān gave his daughter, as in the previous night. It stands in the sentence like an appositive name.

sentences.t: فَأَجَابَهُ الْحَاجِبُ بِالسَّمْعِ وَالطَّاعَةِ وَجَهَّزَ شَرْكَانُ الْجِمَالَ وَالْبِغَالَ وَكَتَبَ كِتَابًا وَسَلَّمَهُ لِلْحَاجِبِ وَوَدَّعَ أُخْتَهُ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ وَكَانَ أَخَذَ مِنْهَا الْخَرَزَةَ وَجَعَلَهَا فِي عُنُقِ ابْنَتِهِ فِي سِلْسِلَةٍ مِنْ خَالِصِ الذَّهَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ajābahu al-ḥājibu bi-al-samʿi wa-al-ṭāʿati wa-jahhaza Sharkānu al-jimāla wa-al-bighāla wa-kataba kitāban wa-sallamahu li-al-ḥājibi wa-waddaʿa ukhtahu Nuzhata al-Zamāni wa-kāna akhadha minhā al-kharazata wa-jaʿalahā fī ʿunuqi ibnatihi fī silsilatin min khāliṣi al-dhahabi
sentences.l: And the chamberlain answered him with hearing and obedience; and Sharkān equipped the camels and the mules, and wrote a letter and handed it to the chamberlain, and bade farewell to his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān. And he had taken from her the bead, and put it on the neck of his daughter, on a chain of pure gold.
sentences.i: The chamberlain answered that he heard and obeyed. Sharkān made ready the camels and mules, wrote a letter and gave it to the chamberlain, and took leave of his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān. He had taken the bead from her and hung it on his daughter’s neck, on a chain of pure gold.
sentences.n: The print marks a shadda on جهّز; kept in place.

sentences.t: وَسَافَرَ الْحَاجِبُ فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّهُ خَرَجَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ وَكَانَ مَعَهُ الْوَقَّادُ يَتَفَرَّجَانِ تَحْتَ الطَّارِمَةِ فَرَأَيَا جِمَالًا وَبَخَاتِيَ وَبِغَالًا مُحَلْمَةً وَمَشَاعِلَ وَفَوَانِيسَ مُضِيئَةً
sentences.tr: wa-sāfara al-ḥājibu fī tilka al-laylati fa-ittafaqa annahu kharaja Ḍawʾu al-Makāni wa-kāna maʿahu al-waqqādu yatafarrajāni taḥta al-ṭārimati fa-raʾayā jimālan wa-bakhātiya wa-bighālan muḥalmatan wa-mashāʿila wa-fawānīsa muḍīʾatan
sentences.l: And the chamberlain travelled in that night, and it happened that Ḍawʾ al-Makān went out, and with him was the fire-tender, the two of them strolling under the pavilion; and they saw camels and Bactrian-camels and mules loaded, and torches and lanterns shining.
sentences.i: The chamberlain set out that same night. It happened that Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the stoker had gone out to stroll beneath the pavilion, and they saw camels, Bactrian camels and mules with their loads, and torches and bright lanterns.
sentences.n: محلمة is printed; it is probably a slip for محملة (muḥammala, “loaded”), the letters transposed, and is rendered so. The vocalisation follows the print. الطارمة is a domed pavilion or porch.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ عَنْ هَذِهِ الْأَحْمَالِ وَعَنْ صَاحِبِهَا فَقَالُوا لَهُ هَذَا خَرَاجُ دِمَشْقَ مُسَافِرٌ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ صَاحِبِ مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾala Ḍawʾu al-Makāni ʿan hādhihi al-aḥmāli wa-ʿan ṣāḥibihā fa-qālū lahu hādhā kharāju Dimashqa musāfirun ilā al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni ṣāḥibi madīnati Baghdāda
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān asked about these loads and about their owner, and they said to him: This is the tribute of Damascus, travelling to the king ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, master of the city of Baghdad.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān asked about the loads and who owned them, and they told him, “This is the tribute of Damascus, going to King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of the city of Baghdad.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَمَنْ هُوَ رَئِيسُ هَذِهِ الْمَحَامِلِ قِيلَ هُوَ الْحَاجِبُ الْكَبِيرُ الَّذِي تَزَوَّجَ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي تَعَلَّمَتِ الْعِلْمَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-man huwa raʾīsu hādhihi al-maḥāmili qīla huwa al-ḥājibu al-kabīru alladhī tazawwaja al-jāriyata allatī taʿallamat al-ʿilma wa-al-ḥikmata
sentences.l: And he said: And who is the chief of these litters? It was said: He is the great chamberlain who married the slave-girl who learned knowledge and wisdom.
sentences.i: He said, “And who is the master of these litters?” They answered, “The chief chamberlain, who married the girl who studied learning and wisdom.”

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَافْتَكَرَ وَتَذَكَّرَ أُمَّهُ وَأَبَاهُ وَأُخْتَهُ وَوَطَنَهُ وَقَالَ لِلْوَقَّادِمَا بَقِيَ لِي هُنَا تَعُودُ بَلْ أُسَافِرُ مَعَ الْقَافِلَةِ هَذِهِ وَأَمْشِي قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا حَتَّى أَصِلَ إِلَى بِلَادِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika bakā bukāʾan shadīdan wa-iftakara wa-tadhakkara ummahu wa-abāhu wa-ukhtahu wa-waṭanahu wa-qāla li-al-waqqādi mā baqiya lī hunā taʿūdu bal usāfiru maʿa al-qāfilati hādhihi wa-amshī qalīlan qalīlan ḥattā aṣila ilā bilādī
sentences.l: And at that, he wept a violent weeping, and thought and remembered his mother and his father and his sister and his homeland, and said to the fire-tender: There remains not for me here a returning; rather I will travel with this caravan, and walk little by little until I arrive at my lands.
sentences.i: At that he wept bitterly. He thought of his mother and his father and his sister and his homeland, and said to the stoker, “There is nothing left for me to come back to here. I will travel with this caravan and walk on, little by little, until I reach my own country.”
sentences.n: ما بقي لي هنا تعود is loosely built; it is read as “there is nothing left for me here to return to (or to stay for)”. The print runs للوقاد and ما together (lil-waqqādimā); kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَقَّادُ أَنَا مَا أَمِنْتُ عَلَيْكَ مِنَ الْقُدْسِ إِلَي دِمَشْقَ فَكَيْفَ آامَنُ عَلَيْكَ إِلَى بَغْدَادَ فَأَنَا أَكُونُ مَعَكَ وَصُحْبَتَكَ حَتَّى تَصِلَ إى مَقْصِدِكَ فَقَالَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-waqqādu anā mā amintu ʿalayka mina al-Quds ilā Dimashqa fa-kayfa a-amanu ʿalayka ilā Baghdāda fa-anā akūnu maʿaka wa-ṣuḥbataka ḥattā taṣila ilā maqṣidika fa-qāla Ḍawʾu al-Makāni ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: And the fire-tender said to him: I did not feel safe for you from Jerusalem to Damascus; so how shall I feel safe for you to Baghdad? So I will be with you, and your companionship, until you reach your goal. And Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: With love and honour.
sentences.i: The stoker said to him, “I was never easy about you from Jerusalem to Damascus — how could I be easy about you as far as Baghdad? I will be with you, in your company, until you reach your goal.” Ḍawʾ al-Makān said, “With love and honour.”
sentences.n: الي and اى are the print’s spellings of إلى; kept as printed. آامن is printed with a madda; it is read as the question أأمن, “shall I be safe?”.

sentences.t: فَشَرَعَ الْوَقَّادُ فِي تَجْهِيزِ حَالِهِ وَشَدَّ لَهُ حِمَارًا وَجَعَلَ خُرْجَهُ عَلَى حِمَارِهِ وَجَعَلَ فِيهِ شَيْأً مِنَ الزَّادِ وَشَدَّ وَسَطَهُ وَتَأَهَّبَ وَوَقَفَ حَتَّى جَازَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْأَحْمَالُ وَالْحَاجِبُ رَاكِبٌ عَلَى هَجِينٍ وَالْمُشَاةُ حَوْلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-sharaʿa al-waqqādu fī tajhīzi ḥālihi wa-shadda lahu ḥimāran wa-jaʿala khurjahu ʿalā ḥimārihi wa-jaʿala fīhi shayʾan mina al-zādi wa-shadda wasaṭahu wa-taʾahhaba wa-waqafa ḥattā jāzat ʿalayhi al-aḥmālu wa-al-ḥājibu rākibun ʿalā hajīnin wa-al-mushātu ḥawlahu
sentences.l: And the fire-tender set about the equipping of his state, and saddled for him a donkey, and put his saddlebag on his donkey, and put in it something of provisions, and tightened his waist, and made ready, and stood until the loads passed by him, and the chamberlain riding on a dromedary and the foot-walkers around him.
sentences.i: The stoker set about getting himself ready. He saddled a donkey for his friend, put his saddlebag on it with some provisions inside, girded his waist and made ready, and stood waiting until the loads had passed by, with the chamberlain riding a swift dromedary and the footmen around him.
sentences.n: The print’s شيأ is a form of شيئا, kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَرَكِبَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ حِمَارَ الْوَقَّادِ وَقَالَ لِلْوَقَّادِا رْكَبْ مَعِي فَقَالَ لَا أَرْكَبُ وَلَكِنْ أَكُونُ فِي خِدْمَتِكَ فَقَالَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ لَابُدَّأَنْ تَرْكَبَ سَاعَةً فَقَالَ لَهُ كَذَلِكَ أَنْ أَتْعَبَ ثُمَّ إِنَّ ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ قَالَ لَهُ سَوْفَ تَنْظُرُ يَا أَخِي مَا أَفْعَلُ بِكَ إِذَا وَصَلْتُ إِلَى أَهْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-rakiba Ḍawʾu al-Makāni ḥimāra al-waqqādi wa-qāla li-al-waqqādi irkab maʿī fa-qāla lā arkabu wa-lākin akūnu fī khidmatika fa-qāla Ḍawʾu al-Makāni lā budda an tarkaba sāʿatan fa-qāla lahu kadhālika an atʿaba thumma inna Ḍawʾa al-Makāni qāla lahu sawfa tanẓuru yā akhī mā afʿalu bika idhā waṣaltu ilā ahlī
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān rode the fire-tender’s donkey and said to the fire-tender: Ride with me. He said: I will not ride, but I will be in your service. Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: You must ride an hour. He said to him: Thus, that I tire. Then Ḍawʾ al-Makān said to him: You will see, O my brother, what I do for you when I reach my family.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān mounted the stoker’s donkey and said, “Ride with me.” “No,” said the stoker, “I will walk and serve you.” “You must ride for an hour,” said Ḍawʾ al-Makān. “Then I shall only tire myself,” he answered. And Ḍawʾ al-Makān said, “Wait, my brother, and you will see what I do for you when I reach my family.”
sentences.n: The print runs للوقاد and ارکب together (lil-waqqādā rkab), and لا بد and أن together (lābuddan); kept as printed. كذلك أن أتعب is obscure and perhaps lacks a particle (a negative or a لـ); it is read tentatively as the stoker giving in grudgingly, “so be it, let me tire”.

sentences.t: وَمَا زَالُوا مُسَافِرِينَ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ فَلَمَّا جَاءَ وَقْتُ الْقَائِلَةِ أَمَرَهُمُ الْحَاجِبُ بِالنُّزُولِ فَنَزَلُوا وَاسْتَرَاحُوا وَأَسْقَوْ جِمَالَهُمْ ثُمَّ أَمَرَهُمْ بِالْمَسِيرِ وَبَعْدَ خَمْسَةِ أَيَّامٍ وَصَلُوا إِلَى مَدِينَةِ حَمَاةَ وَنَزَلُوا فَأَقَامُوا بِهَا ثَلْثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zālū musāfirīna ilā an ṭalaʿati al-shamsu fa-lammā jāʾa waqtu al-qāʾilati amarahumu al-ḥājibu bi-al-nuzūli fa-nazalū wa-istarāḥū wa-asqaw jimālahum thumma amarahum bi-al-masīri wa-baʿda khamsati ayyāmin waṣalū ilā madīnati Ḥamāta wa-nazalū fa-aqāmū bihā thalthata ayyāmin
sentences.l: And they did not cease travelling until the sun rose; and when the time of the noon-rest came, the chamberlain commanded them with the alighting, and they alighted and rested and watered their camels; then he commanded them with the journeying. And after five days they arrived at the city of Ḥamāh and alighted, and stayed in it three days.
sentences.i: They went on travelling until the sun rose, and when it was time for the midday rest the chamberlain ordered them to halt. They halted, rested and watered their camels, and then he ordered them on. After five days they reached the city of Ḥamāh, halted, and stayed there three days.
sentences.n: The print’s اسقو is a spelling of أسقوا (final alif omitted), and ثلثة of ثلاثة; kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُ—بَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The stock close of a night. The print’s last word is damaged (الم—باح, with a dash inside it); it is read as the formula’s usual al-mubāḥ.
